title: Begin with the Viking world
intro: Build a broad foundation before choosing a specialist question.
steps: Start with the museum’s overview and explore an object that interests you.
Compare the regional story in England with the broader museum view.
Bring unfree people into the picture when thinking about wealth and expansion.
Take up a book-length synthesis and use its references to pursue a question.
question: Whose lives are easiest to see in the surviving evidence—and whose are harder to recover?

title: Read the gods through their sources
intro: Move from an introduction to the poems and prose behind familiar stories.
steps: Learn what kinds of sources survive before reading a modern retelling.
Choose a poem, then read its introduction and notes as well as its translation.
Compare how a prose account organizes the mythological material.
Compare the wording of a shared poem across translations.
question: Which parts of your reading come from a medieval witness, and which come from a modern editor or translator?

title: Sagas, manuscripts and words
intro: Follow a story from a readable edition towards the witnesses and language behind it.
steps: Begin with one saga and record its title and translator.
Read a modern study for social and regional context.
Explore the catalogue and notice the copying dates of manuscripts.
Use a dictionary to investigate a word in context.
Try a specialist poetry record and identify its editor.
Explore an inscription and preserve its identifier when taking notes.
question: How does the kind of text change what you can reasonably ask it to tell you?

title: Ships, routes and distant shores
intro: Connect vessels with the places, trade and evidence of travel.
steps: Examine the difference between surviving ship parts and a reconstruction.
Place maritime travel alongside a trading town and land routes.
Read the official record for the Newfoundland site.
Follow the dating study, paying attention to the exact claim supported by the method.
question: What does each source establish about travel, and what does it leave unresolved?

title: Households, wealth and power
intro: Broaden the view beyond raids to social relationships, objects and public claims.
steps: Use objects to begin asking questions about everyday activity.
Include coercion and inequality when considering Viking society.
Ask how an object’s life might differ from the moment it was buried.
Compare monumental claims with their archaeological setting.
Read a regional social history in greater depth.
question: How do wealth, authority and status appear differently in texts, objects and monuments?

title: Learn to read a discovery
intro: Work from accessible explanations towards methods, interpretation and debate.
steps: Separate a survey detection from subsequent confirmation and dating.
Follow a research project that asks questions about objects and their wrapping.
Distinguish analytical findings from an argument about a person’s life.
Identify exactly what the dating method measures.
Use a project bibliography to move from overview to specialist report.
question: For each claim, can you name the observation, the method and the interpretive step?
